sudo /opt/voyager/governor.py close             # close now (by hand)

Rollout test (rollout step 5):

  1. Lower the threshold: echo GOVERNOR_CLOSE_GIB=0.001 | sudo tee -a /etc/voyager/governor.env, then wait a minute.
  2. Confirm from outside (your laptop) that curl -m 10 https://<host>/health fails.
  3. Confirm the email and the uptime alert arrive.
  4. Remove the line from /etc/voyager/governor.env and run sudo /opt/voyager/governor.py apply. Check that status shows open and the site answers again.

docs.title: 9. Domain
docs.text:
The site starts on <a-b-c-d>.sslip.io. The certificates live in the persistent caddy_data volume, so restarts don't hit Let's Encrypt's duplicate limit. To move to your own domain:

  1. Add an A record pointing at the static IP. Add no AAAA record: IPv6 egress would be Premium tier, outside the free 200 GiB.
  2. gcloud compute instances add-metadata voyager-vm --zone=us-east1-b --metadata=voyager-site-host=your.domain
  3. On the VM: sudo google_metadata_script_runner startup. This rewrites site.env and app.env's URLs; restart Caddy in a quiet moment.
  4. Update the Android PROD_BASE_URL and the uptime check's host.

docs.title: Moving to a custom domain
docs.text:
Everything absolute comes from PUBLIC_BASE_URL (else APP_BASE_URL), so the move is configuration only:

  1. DNS: an A record to the static IP, no AAAA (as above).
  2. Set voyager-site-host (step 2 above) and run the startup script on the VM: it rewrites SITE_HOST for Caddy and APP_BASE_URL/CORS_ORIGINS in app.env. If you set PUBLIC_BASE_URL in app.env, change it too. Restart the app.
  3. Provider consoles: add the new redirect URI https://<domain>/api/auth/oauth/<p>/callback for every provider (keep the old one until the old host is retired), and update Apple's domain and return URL. Email links follow the new base automatically.
  4. Mobile deep links (Phases 7 and 8): the iOS apple-app-site-association and Android assetlinks.json files are served from the new domain's /.well-known/. Universal and app links only work on a domain you own.
  5. Keep the old <ip>.sslip.io host answering with a redirect to the new domain for a while so old emails, shares and bookmarks still work. Pending verify and reset links issued before the move point at the old host; they expire in 30 minutes.

Known limitation: Google does not accept sslip.io. Google OAuth rejects redirect URIs on public-suffix domains such as sslip.io, so Google sign-in becomes available only after the move to a custom domain. GitHub, Facebook, Apple (needs a verified domain) and email sign-in are unaffected. Until then the Google button shows "coming soon".

docs.title: Sign-in providers and email
docs.text:
Providers are config-gated: add the credentials, restart the app, and the provider turns on with no client update. The redirect (callback) URI to register in each provider's console is <PUBLIC_BASE_URL>/api/auth/oauth/<p>/callback, where <p> is google, github, facebook or apple, for example https://34-23-1-2.sslip.io/api/auth/oauth/github/callback. Client IDs go in /opt/voyager/app.env (uncomment the lines in app.env.example); secrets go in Secret Manager (google-client-secret, github-client-secret, facebook-app-secret, apple-private-key, created empty by the bootstrap) with the same printf/read -s pattern as section 3.

  • GitHub: Settings → Developer settings → OAuth Apps → New. Callback URL as above. Set GITHUB_CLIENT_ID and github-client-secret.
  • Facebook: developers.facebook.com → create an app with Facebook Login, add the callback under Valid OAuth Redirect URIs. Set FACEBOOK_APP_ID and facebook-app-secret. Facebook's email is untrusted unless FACEBOOK_EMAIL_TRUSTED=true.
  • Google: Google Cloud console → APIs & Services → Credentials → OAuth client ID (Web). Needs a custom domain (see the limitation above). Add the iOS and Android client IDs to GOOGLE_NATIVE_CLIENT_IDS for the native apps.
  • Apple: in the Apple developer account create an App ID with Sign in with Apple, then a Services ID (this is APPLE_SERVICES_ID; enable Sign in with Apple, set the verified domain and the callback URL above, which Apple calls with a form POST). Create a Key with Sign in with Apple enabled: its Key ID is APPLE_KEY_ID, the downloaded .p8 contents go in the apple-private-key secret, and your Team ID is APPLE_TEAM_ID. Add the app bundle IDs to APPLE_NATIVE_CLIENT_IDS.
  • SMTP: sign-up verification and password reset need working email. Set the app's SMTP_HOST, SMTP_PORT (587), SMTP_USERNAME, SMTP_FROM in app.env and the smtp-password secret (section 3). Without SMTP, GET /api/config reports signup_available: false and the sign-up and reset forms are hidden. Sign-up also needs SIGNUP_ENABLED=true: setting SMTP alone (for example for fare alerts) enables password reset but never opens public sign-up.
  • SIGNUP_MODE: open (default) or invite. In invite mode, create codes with POST /api/admin/invites (admin only); each code has a use limit and an expiry.

docs.title: 10. Cost watch
docs.text:
• Budgets (pre-tax, in INR): "Voyager total (alerts)" at ₹2,300 sends email at 50/90/100 % and on forecast; "Voyager Gemini spend cap" at ₹1,800 pauses Gemini when reached. Billing data can lag a day; the on-box governor doesn't.
  • Monthly check: in Billing → Reports, filter on the project. Expect about $3.65 for the IP, cents for snapshots, $0 for egress and Gemini as used. Also check governor.py status, and in GCS that the bucket holds a few MB with no soft-deleted bytes.
  • Never add: a load balancer, Cloud NAT, Cloud Run, Artifact Registry (image scanning), a logging agent, external IPv6, or a second VM.
  • SerpAPI (free plan, 250 searches/month): FARE_WATCH_DAILY_CALL_BUDGET=6 in app.env.

docs.title: Site down, app stuck starting: net.ipv4.ip_forward is 0
docs.text:
Symptoms. The site doesn't answer on 80/443, the uptime check fires, and the app container hangs in its entrypoint because it can't reach the metadata server or Secret Manager. Docker itself looks healthy.

Check:

cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward      # must print 1
journalctl -u voyager-governor | grep ip_forward
ls /etc/sysctl.d/                      # 99-voyager-docker.conf must be there

Fix by hand (the governor does this within a minute):

sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1

Why it happens. Docker needs IPv4 forwarding for its published ports (DNAT) and for the containers' own outbound traffic. It turns forwarding on only when dockerd starts. The GCE Debian image ships /etc/sysctl.d/60-gce-network-security.conf with net.ipv4.ip_forward=0, so any full sysctl reload under a running Docker turns forwarding off again. That includes sysctl --system and a restart of systemd-sysctl, for example by a package upgrade.

Incident 2026-11-06, about 17:15 UTC (about 10 minutes down). Re-running the startup script after --update-host reached sysctl --system in first-boot.sh (configure_memory). That reload re-applied the image's ip_forward=0. Docker was already running, and the re-run doesn't restart it, so forwarding stayed off: the app couldn't fetch its secrets, and inbound traffic was dropped. The hot-fix on the VM was /etc/sysctl.d/99-voyager-docker.conf (net.ipv4.ip_forward=1) plus sysctl --system.

What prevents it now:

  • first-boot.sh writes /etc/sysctl.d/99-voyager-docker.conf before anything applies sysctl settings. The file sorts after 60-…, so it wins at boot and on every reload.
  • first-boot.sh applies only its own files (sysctl -p <file>) and never runs sysctl --system.
  • /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/99-voyager-ipfwd, also written by first-boot.sh, is a DPkg::Post-Invoke hook. After every dpkg run, unattended upgrades included, it re-applies only 99-voyager-docker.conf. That covers a package postinst that applies just the image's 60-… file, which bypasses the file ordering.
  • The governor's per-minute guard sets forwarding back to 1 and emails you (section 8). It also keeps the FORWARD policy at DROP.
  • CI's first_boot_sim.sh (job host-checks) installs the image's 60-gce-network-security.conf. It then runs a first boot, a re-run on the live VM and a reboot, and checks after each that forwarding stays 1. It also runs a real apt-get in which a simulated postinst applies the 60-… file alone, and checks that the hook restores 1.

docs.title: Share-link previews (crawler route)
docs.text: Caddy rewrites /share/<token> to the app's /api/share/<token>/page for link-preview crawlers only (fixed User-Agent list in deploy/gcp/Caddyfile, @crawler); everyone else gets the SPA. If the app answers 4xx/5xx (revoked or unknown token, SHARING_V2_ENABLED=false, an app build without the route) Caddy falls back to the SPA index.html, so a link never breaks and no app change is needed to roll back. Check by hand: curl -A facebookexternalhit/1.1 https://<host>/share/<token> should show og: tags, and without the -A the SPA. Set PUBLIC_BASE_URL in app.env so the tags carry the public host. Contract: Sharing API.

docs.title: Deploys: the SPA, Caddy or the deployer
docs.text:
• New SPA not showing. journalctl -u voyager-deploy -n 50. skipping Caddy … held means a digest failed a check: the email and the log say why. Release it by deleting its line in /opt/voyager/failed-digests, or merge a fix (a newer digest ends the hold). release: … lines name the check that refused the image (symlink, missing asset, size).
  • Caddyfile … does not validate. The new Caddyfile failed caddy adapt --validate with the real SITE_HOST; nothing was switched. Fix it in deploy/gcp/Caddyfile. To test on the VM by hand: sudo docker run --rm --network none -e SITE_HOST=… -e ACME_EMAIL=… -v /var/lib/voyager/edge:/edge:ro --entrypoint caddy <CADDY_IMAGE> adapt --config /edge/current/Caddyfile --adapter caddyfile --validate.
  • Caddy won't start, /edge/current/Caddyfile: no such file. The edge directory is missing or broken. Run sudo /opt/voyager/deploy.sh: before anything else it rebuilds current from the image pinned in images.env, with no registry needed. It refuses to touch Caddy if it can't, and emails you.
  • GHCR back-off until …. GHCR answered 429. The deployer only converges until the back-off ends. To clear it at once: sudo rm /run/voyager-deploy/backoff.
  • A merge didn't reach the VM. Look at the Deploy run. promote-app / promote-caddy skipped: ci or that image's build job failed (a failed Trivy scan fails the build job; bump the base or the dependency, or, for an accepted finding, add it to .trivyignore with a reason). The other image is promoted regardless. main moved on to …: a newer merge will publish instead. app unchanged (inputs …) / caddy unchanged: that image's inputs equal the prod image's, so nothing was built and prod stayed, by design. prod moved to … while this run kept …: prod changed under the run (only possible by hand); re-run the workflow. could not read main's HEAD: GitHub didn't answer git ls-remote; re-run.
  • Prod scan failed (prod-scan.yml). A fixed CRITICAL vulnerability is live. Merge the fix (e.g. a base image bump), or if it's in the base image or a pip dependency, run Deploy by hand: the forced rebuild picks up the newest base and dependencies.
  • A deploy recreated Caddy unexpectedly. Look for Caddy runtime changed (… → …) (a new base image digest or caddy.Dockerfile runtime change) or compose config of Caddy changed (a new compose.yaml). Both drain open streams first, for up to 90 s.

docs.title: Rollout of auto-deploy on the existing VM (once)
docs.text:
The VM still runs the old deployer, with the SPA baked into the Caddy image and a weekly Caddy window. Order matters:

  1. Merge, and wait for the Deploy workflow. The old deployer deploys the new app (it has /internal/streams) and only stages the new Caddy image (new Caddy staged for the night window). The new image is safe even if the old Sunday window applies it under the old compose.yaml: without the edge mount, /edge/current in the image points at its own SPA and Caddyfile.
  2. infrastructure/gcp/bootstrap.sh --update-host voyager-prod-ohzkl 010A0B-F39593-14A899 <alert email>.
  3. On the VM: sudo google_metadata_script_runner startup. first-boot.sh unpacks the kit under the deploy lock (so a timer run never mixes old and new files), creates /var/lib/voyager/edge (root, 0755), restarts voyager-deploy.timer on its new 60 s schedule and runs the new deploy.sh. Expected in journalctl -u google-startup-scripts -u voyager-deploy:
  4. edge: no current release; extracting it from … (the running image's SPA, kept as an asset fallback)
  5. verifying …, pulling …, then Caddy runtime changed ( → <id>): recreating Caddy
  6. drain: no open streams (or … still open after 90s; recreating Caddy anyway)
  7. Caddy healthy on the new runtime: release …
  8. Downtime: one Caddy recreate, about 2–5 s of refused connections. Open streams are drained first for up to 90 s. Certificates stay in caddy_data. The app isn't restarted by the update. If you ran --update-host before the new image was published, Caddy is recreated once for the new compose.yaml, still serving the old SPA, and once more when the first labelled image arrives.
  9. Check: sudo cat /opt/voyager/images.env has CADDY_CONTENT_IMAGE=; ls -l /var/lib/voyager/edge shows current; systemctl list-timers voyager-deploy.timer shows a 1-minute cadence; cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward prints 1; curl -m 10 https://<host>/health answers. Then merge a frontend-only change and watch SPA live: release … with no Caddy restart (docker ps shows Caddy's uptime unchanged).

docs.title: Production: one e2-micro VM on GCP
docs.text:
Production runs on a single always-free e2-micro VM in us-east1 (project voyager-prod-ohzkl). Caddy terminates TLS and serves the SPA, the app container runs FastAPI with SQLite on the VM's persistent disk, and Gemini on Vertex AI is called with the VM's service account. Hosting costs about $4 a month; Gemini is capped by a spend cap.

  • Runbook: Deployment on GCP covers bootstrap, secrets, first boot, the data migration, deploys and rollback, restore drills, the egress governor and cost watch.
  • Design: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-06-gcp-lean-deploy-design.md.
  • Files:
Path What deploy/gcp/compose.yaml app + caddy, images pinned by digest, memory limits, log rotation, health checks deploy/gcp/Caddyfile, deploy/gcp/caddy.Dockerfile TLS, SPA caching, /api + /health proxy (SSE-safe); the Caddy image bakes in the built SPA deploy/gcp/app.env.example non-secret app settings on the VM deploy/gcp/host/ first-boot.sh (provisioning), deploy.sh (signed-digest deployer with rollback), governor.py (egress governor), window.sh, systemd units infrastructure/gcp/bootstrap.sh idempotent gcloud bootstrap (--dry-run, --update-host) infrastructure/gcp/migrate_old_prod.py strips the 2026-08-30 export to the users and their data .github/workflows/deploy.yml on every green merge to main: build, push to GHCR, sign with cosign, move prod

The VM pulls; CI never has access to it.

docs.title: History
docs.text: The first production ran on Cloud Run (Terraform + a push deploy workflow) from 2026-05 until it was decommissioned on 2026-08-30. That Terraform, its scripts and the old workflow were removed in the VM deployment change; git history keeps them.

docs.title: Running locally
docs.text:
./start.sh                       # dev servers on :8001 and :5174
# or
docker compose up --build        # containers on :8001 and :8080

See Setup and Installation. The documentation site is published separately by docs.yml (see Testing and CI).

docs.title: Deploying elsewhere
docs.text:
Any host that can run the containers works. Requirements:

  • One backend process. Rate limits and the SQLite file are per-process. Give it a persistent volume for DATA_DIR. On a single VM like ours, set BACKUP_MODE=vm with a BACKUP_BUCKET and a marker file (DATA_DIR/.voyager-data-disk). On a host with an ephemeral disk, the legacy BACKUP_MODE=cloudrun restores at every start and merges.
  • Secrets. JWT_SECRET_KEY is required (python -m app.entrypoint refuses to start without it) and so is ADMIN_PASSWORD. LLM credentials depend on the provider. SERPAPI_KEY and SERPER_KEY are optional. They come from the environment, or from Secret Manager through SECRET_MANAGER_SECRETS.
  • Origins. Set CORS_ORIGINS to the frontend's origin. Serve the SPA and /api from the same origin, as Caddy here or nginx in frontend/.
  • Behind a proxy. Set FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS to the proxy's address or network (never *), so rate limits key on real client IPs. In production set ALLOW_ANONYMOUS_AI=false.
  • SSE. The proxy must not buffer or compress text/event-stream. The app sends a keepalive every 15 s.
  • Fare and price watches run inside the backend process when SERPAPI_KEY is set. Keep one worker. Size FARE_WATCH_DAILY_CALL_BUDGET to your SerpAPI plan.
  • Alert emails need SMTP_* and APP_BASE_URL set to the public URL, whose host must proxy /api.

docs.title: Frontend
docs.text: A React 18 single-page app built with Vite 6, React Router 6 (react-router-dom 6.28) and Tailwind CSS 3.4. Maps use Leaflet with react-leaflet, icons come from lucide-react, and HTTP goes through axios. @tanstack/react-query provides a QueryClientProvider in main.jsx. What the user sees is described in Trip Planning Features; this page covers how the code is organised.

docs.title: Routing and always-mounted tabs
docs.text:
Routes in App.jsx:

Path Page Access /login LoginPage Public /share/:token SharePage Public /change-password ChangePasswordPage Signed in / SearchPage, then ResultsPage Signed in /chat ChatPage Signed in /nearby NearbyPage Signed in /trips, /explore, /play, /you TripsPage, Search and Results, PlayPage, YouPage Signed in, only with features.journey /trips/:id (/:tab) TripPage Signed in, only with features.journey /alerts AlertsPage (?watch=ID, &replan=1) Signed in /preferences PreferencesPage Signed in /admin AdminPage Admins (RequireAdmin) anything else redirect to /

Search/Results and Chat are always mounted and hidden with CSS, so navigating away never loses streaming results, a half-typed message or a response in progress. Preferences, Near me, Alerts and Admin mount on each visit (Near me's live results are dropped when you leave it). SearchDataProvider sits inside the signed-in Layout, so logging out discards all search state. A user flagged requires_password_change is redirected to /change-password. AttributionFooter renders the GeoNames and OurAirports credit under every page. Each route change sends a page-view analytics event, and the telemetry SDK records a screen view. LoginPage shows SocialSignInButtons, which ask GET /api/auth/providers (the endpoint does not exist yet): a 404, an empty list or an unconfigured provider shows "coming soon" (OAuth itself arrives in Phase 1). ConsentPrompt shows the one-time telemetry choice where consent is required.

docs.title: State
docs.text:
• AuthContext keeps the JWT (localStorage['tp_token']), the user (username, is_admin, requires_password_change) and the saved preferences. It loads preferences after login and writes Search-form values back to them on submit (the two-way binding).
  • AlertsContext (inside the signed-in Layout) polls GET /api/notifications/unread-count every 60 s while the tab is visible (stopped while hidden, refreshed on return and focus), turns a newly arrived alert into one toast or, when the window isn't focused and permission was granted, a native notification, and caches each trip's watch for the "Watch fare" buttons. Outside the provider useAlerts() is inert, so components keep rendering in isolation.
  • SearchDataContext holds the search form, the streamed results and per-agent status, shared by SearchPage and ResultsPage.
  • Plan selections, itinerary overlays and planner settings are local state in ResultsPage and ChatPage.
  • Grounded live answers (Near me and "Search the web now") are component state only: never in context, browser storage or the React Query cache.

docs.title: Streaming workers
docs.text: sseWorker.js POSTs to /api/search, reads the body as a stream, splits data: events, and posts each parsed event to the main thread, which only updates React state. If the stream closes without a done event it posts __interrupted. chatWorker.js does the same for /api/chat. Keeping the parsing off the main thread keeps the UI responsive while large payloads arrive.

docs.title: API layer
docs.text: services/api.js is an axios instance that adds Authorization: Bearer <token>, plus helpers: streamSearch (spawns the worker), the filtered searches, fetchFareCalendar, getSerpapiConfigured (reads /health once per page load), discoverDestinations, the recent-search calls, compareDestination and recheckStressTest. utils/httpError.js turns error responses into messages, showing a string detail (such as the 429 rate-limit message) as-is.

docs.title: Price alerts 2.0
docs.text: components/alerts2/ is rendered only when useAlertsV2 says so: features.price_alerts_v2 from /api/config is true, or features.alerts_api === 2 and localStorage.tp_alerts2 = "1" ("0" always turns it off). Against a backend without features.alerts_api the classic Alerts page renders and no v2 control appears. Each watch card gets a price story (inline-SVG chart, keyboard-scrubbable, typical range, target slider, verdict and advice translated from codes plus params), the Alerts page a savings tally with milestones and a shareable "I caught $X" card (Canvas 2D, Web Share API), the notification bell a drop moment card (count-up skipped under prefers-reduced-motion) and the preferences panel the digest, quiet-hour, cap and grouping controls. One-tap watch and the suggestions sheet appear on Results, Chat and Trip cards and are hidden when features.live_prices is false. The Deal-hunter track follows the account's hide_game setting. Strings live in the priceStory, savings, quickWatch, watchSuggest, alertPrefs and alertsHub namespaces, plus added keys in alerts and game. AlertsContext also surfaces a drop's data.drop and data.game.

docs.title: Utilities
docs.text:
Pure, unit-tested helpers in src/utils/:

Module Purpose analytics.js Batches UI events and posts them to /api/analytics/events (every 5 s or 10 events) bestValuePackage.js Rule-based best-value picks budgetPlanner.js Budget split and fit checks chatHistory.js Text stand-ins for structured chat turns compare.js Compare-mode requests and table model fareCalendar.js Fare-calendar cells and date shifting geo.js Great-circle distance (haversineKm) httpError.js Error messages from API responses itineraryLayout.js Drag-and-drop overlay (arrangeItinerary, fingerprints) orderSectionByCity.js Stable sort of multi-city lists into journey order planExport.js .ics export planHelpers.js Plan cost, cost breakdown, names, counts planPrint.js Print/PDF page recentSearches.js Recent-search formatting and date roll-forward remix.js Trip Remix presets schedule.js Estimated start/end times (scheduleDays) stressTestPayload.js Payload for the health-check re-check tour.js Onboarding-tour completion flag verification.js Resolving pending badges, stripping link evidence from saved plans

docs.title: Maps
docs.text: TripMap.jsx renders the itinerary with Leaflet and OpenStreetMap tiles: numbered markers per activity stop, a dashed polyline in visit order, popups, and fitBounds on the activity area. The chat page draws its own map in the same style for city markers and place pins, and leaves the origin out of the bounds so the view does not zoom out across continents.

docs.title: Dev server and production build
docs.text:
• npm run dev starts Vite on port 5174. vite.config.js proxies /api and /health to http://localhost:8001.
  • npm run build writes dist/. The container (frontend/Dockerfile) builds with node:20-alpine and serves dist/ from nginx:alpine on port 8080. nginx.conf.template proxies /api/ and /health to BACKEND_URL, with buffering off for SSE and a 120 s read timeout.
  • The app uses no VITE_* environment variables.

docs.title: Travel Planner — Developer Docs
docs.text:
Travel Planner turns a route, travel dates, a budget and a list of interests into a complete trip plan. A team of Claude agents builds the plan, and the results stream to the browser section by section as each agent finishes.

These pages are the technical documentation for people working on the code. The project is open source under the MIT License (LICENSE at the repo root).

Hosting. Production deploys to a single always-free e2-micro VM on GCP (Caddy + the app container, SQLite on the disk, about $4 a month); every green merge to main deploys. See Deployment on GCP. To try the app yourself, run it locally with ./start.sh or docker compose up --build (see Setup and Installation).

docs.title: What the app does
docs.text:
• Search in three modes: I know where I'm going (one city or up to 3 stops on the way), Surprise me (5 suggested destinations), and Compare (2–3 destinations side by side). Recent searches are kept per user.
  • Results: 16 sections (flights, weather, hotels, activities, places to see, free walking tours, events, visa, SIM, tips, emergency card, getting around, forex, itinerary, trip health check and packing list), each with a source-verification label.
  • Planning tools on the Results page: a best-value package, a client-side budget planner, an opt-in fare calendar with Google Flights price insights, Trip Remix presets, and an itinerary you can rearrange by drag-and-drop with estimated times, edits, notes and a re-check.
  • My Plan drawer: pick items into a plan, see the cost breakdown, export to calendar (.ics) or print/PDF, save plans and share them by public link.
  • Chat: a travel advisor that answers from model knowledge and can plan a whole trip in the conversation.
  • Personalization: saved preferences bound two ways to the Search form, and a Taste Graph learned from saved plans.
  • Accounts: sign-up with email verification, Google, GitHub, Facebook and Apple sign-in (config-gated), admin-created users, an admin page, a feedback widget and per-user rate limits.

Trip Planning Features describes each of these in detail.

docs.title: How a search works, in brief
docs.text:
1. Phase 0 (instant). Static lookup tables yield visa, SIM, tips, getting-around and forex results, the Travel Ease confidence grade and the emergency card, all marked source: "static".
  2. Phase 1 (parallel AI). Thirteen specialist agents run concurrently and stream their results as they finish. For the six static-backed agents (visa, sim, tips, getting_around, forex, emergency_card) an AI failure is suppressed, so the static data stays on screen. Two deferred agents, packing list and pricing advisor, start as soon as their inputs are ready.
  3. Phase 2. The itinerary agent starts once activities and hotels are in (60 s timeout, template fallback). When the itinerary is final, the stress-test agent audits it.

Every specialist agent uses Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite on Vertex AI through BaseAgent. Chat uses Gemini 3.8 Flash for conversational answers. Without GCP_PROJECT and with an Anthropic key (or LLM_PROVIDER=anthropic) both use Claude (Haiku 4.5 / Sonnet 4.6). See Architecture and Agent System.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text: Page What it covers Setup and Installation Running locally with start.sh, by hand, or with Docker Compose; first login Configuration Every environment variable and its default Architecture Components, orchestration phases, SSE, persistence, caching, rate limits Agent System The 22 agent definitions, BaseAgent, static fallbacks, verification Trip Planning Features Search modes, every Results section, planning tools, itinerary, My Plan Multi-City Trips Stops, day allocation, per-leg flights, per-city coverage Chat Assistant Routing, knowledge-first answers, comprehensive planning, refinement Personalization Preferences, recent searches, search dials, Taste Graph Sharing and Plans My Plan drawer, saved plans, export, share links Place and Airport Data OurAirports and GeoNames data, licences, how typed places resolve to airports Frontend React app structure, routing, contexts, workers, utilities API Reference Every endpoint, SSE event types, rate-limit buckets Testing and CI Test commands, lint gates, GitHub Actions workflows Deployment Production on one GCP VM, the deploy pipeline, and deploying elsewhere Deployment on GCP Runbook: bootstrap, secrets, first boot, migration, rollback, restore drills, egress governor, cost watch Contributing Workflow, code style, adding an agent Changelog Merged PRs by theme, and the history before them

docs.title: Links
docs.text:
• GitHub repository
  • Project homepage
  • Open an issue

Place data contains data from GeoNames (geonames.org), CC BY 4.0. Airport data comes from OurAirports (public domain). See Place and Airport Data.

docs.title: Internationalization
docs.text: The web app ships in seven languages: English (en), Spanish (es), German (de), French (fr), Hindi (hi), Simplified Chinese (zh) and Bengali (bn). Translations are machine-drafted and reviewed by a second model; native-speaker review of Hindi, Bengali and Chinese is recommended before promoting the app in those languages.

docs.title: Catalogue
docs.text:
Strings live in frontend/src/i18n/locales/<lang>/<namespace>.json, loaded with i18next 26 and react-i18next 17.

Namespace Holds common Navigation, buttons, theme and language labels, shared words search Search page (modes, form, recent searches, compare, from-a-link) results Results page and budget planner chat Chat page plan My Plan drawer, cost breakdown, export itinerary Itinerary and timeline alerts Fare and price alerts account Preferences, change password, share auth Login and social sign-in buttons sections Result section chrome (flights, hotels, visa, ...) privacy Consent prompt and Privacy switch adminTelemetry Admin Analytics tab journey Journey tabs, trips hub shell and load states offline Offline banner, queued-write messages trips, trip, today, prep, completeness Trips hub, trip screen, Today view, prep checklist, trip-ready meter offlinePack, expenses, journal, recap Offline pack, expenses, journal and place ratings, recap coach, explore, nearbyTrip, playYou Coach marks, Explore header, Near me trip actions, Play and You tabs misc Everything else

English is lazy per route: common, errors, auth, journey, offline and misc, plus the namespaces the shell renders at first paint, ship in the main bundle; the rest (for example trip, trips, prep, expenses, journal, recap) load when their route is opened (frontend/src/i18n/routeNamespaces.js). The other six languages always load on demand.

Conventions:

  • Keys are nested objects, referenced as ns:area.thing (for example common:nav.search). In a component: const { t } = useTranslation('common').
  • Interpolation is {{name}}. Markup inside a string uses <tag> placeholders with Trans.
  • Plurals use the i18next JSON v4 suffixes on the key: nights_one, nights_other, and the further forms a language needs (_few, _many, ...), selected by {{count}}.
  • Brand names (Apple, Google, Facebook, GitHub) are not translated. Data returned by the AI is not part of the catalogue.

docs.title: Adding a string
docs.text:
1. Add the key to en/<ns>.json (a new namespace is just a new file in en/; it is discovered automatically).
  2. Add the same key to the other six languages' files.
  3. Run cd frontend && NODE_OPTIONS=--experimental-require-module npx vitest run src/i18n (on Node 20.18; plain npx vitest run elsewhere).

src/i18n/catalog.test.js enforces for every namespace and language: valid JSON; exactly the en keys; plural forms equal to the language's Intl.PluralRules categories; no empty or non-string value; no value equal to its key; the same {{placeholders}} and <tags> as en (a plural form may drop {{count}}); and no file outside en's namespaces.

docs.title: Loading and detection
docs.text:
src/i18n/index.js: English is bundled for every namespace; the other six languages are separate chunks fetched on first use, and while a chunk loads English shows (no Suspense). A missing chunk (offline, stale deploy) leaves English in place.

The language is chosen from localStorage['tp_lang'], else navigator.languages (base tag: zh-TW becomes zh), else en. setLanguage(code) switches, stores tp_lang and emits language_change. The picker is LanguagePicker (NavBar and Preferences, data-tid="nav.language"), listing languages by their native names. <html lang> follows the language (zh-CN, hi-IN and bn-IN for the Intl APIs; others the bare code).

Noto Sans Devanagari (hi), Noto Sans Bengali (bn) and Noto Sans SC (zh) are fetched from Google Fonts the first time one of those languages is used, and placed after Inter and Sora in the font stacks.

docs.title: Formatting
docs.text:
src/i18n/format.js wraps Intl and follows the current language; each helper falls back to a readable value instead of throwing:

Helper Use fmtNumber(n, opts) Numbers fmtCurrency(n, currency) Currency amounts fmtDate(d, opts) Dates and times (empty string for an invalid date) fmtRelative(ms) Signed offset from now, "3 hours ago" or "in 2 days" (under a minute reads as "now")

docs.title: AI output
docs.text:
The web app adds locale (the base language code) to AI-calling requests (localeField() in services/api.js): POST /api/search, /chat, /discover, /compare/destination, /stress-test and the single-agent and /filtered routes. When it is not en, BaseAgent.execute appends an instruction to the agent's system prompt asking for every human-readable value in that language while keeping JSON keys, enum values, codes, URLs, prices, currency codes, dates and place names as in English. Absent or en leaves prompts unchanged. The search cache keeps a separate entry per language (English keys are unchanged). Field and wire format: API Reference.

The static Phase 0 tables (visa, SIM, tips, getting around, forex, emergency card) stay in English until the AI result replaces them; only the UI around them is translated.

docs.title: For other clients
docs.text: The catalogue is the web's source for now. Android and iOS get their own generated resources in later phases (see Feature Parity). The language set and the locale request field are shared by all clients.

docs.title: Multi-City Trips
docs.text: Travel Planner supports full multi-stop journeys — e.g. New York → Paris → Rome → Barcelona → New York — with every section of the results page covering every stop, in the exact order you entered them.

docs.title: Requesting a multi-city trip
docs.text:
The "To" city is the final destination; any added stops are intermediate cities visited on the way there. The destinations list is the full journey in travel order — stops first, final destination last — and destination is that final city:

{
  "origin": "NYC",
  "destination": "Barcelona",
  "destinations": ["Paris", "Rome", "Barcelona"],
  "departure_date": "2026-09-10",
  "return_date": "2026-09-19",
  "destination_nights": [2, 3, null],
  "nationality": "American"
}

destination_nights is optional and aligned with destinations: set exact nights for any stop and leave the rest null — unspecified cities (typically the final destination) share the remaining days automatically.

On the Search page, enter your final destination in To, then add up to 3 stops in the order you'll pass through them (4 cities in all); each stop has an optional nights field (1–30).

Single-city only: the fare calendar, Google's price insights and Compare mode work only for single-destination trips. POST /api/flights/fare-calendar and POST /api/compare/destination answer multi-city requests with 422.

docs.title: How days are allocated — city_stays
docs.text:
Cities with explicit destination_nights get exactly those days; the remaining days are split proportionally across the rest (TravelSearchRequest.city_stays in backend/app/schemas/request.py). With no nights specified, an N-city trip of D days uses round(i × D / N) boundaries so every date is covered exactly once regardless of how unevenly the division falls:

City Start End (move-on day) Nights Paris Sep 10 Sep 13 3 Rome Sep 13 Sep 16 3 Barcelona Sep 16 Sep 19 3

Each stay's end_date is the day the traveler moves on — it equals the next city's start_date, and the last city's end is the return date.

docs.title: Flights — one search per leg
docs.text:
flight_legs decomposes the journey into one-way legs: origin → city₁ on the departure date, an inter-city hop on each move-on day, and last city → origin on the return date.

The flights pipeline (backend/app/services/serp_flights.py::search_multi_city) then:

  1. Resolves every endpoint to up to 3 scheduled airport codes with lookup_city_iata (local database only; see Place and Airport Data). A city that is ambiguous, such as "Valencia" without a country, resolves to nothing, and that leg falls back to an AI estimate.
  2. Fires parallel one-way Google Flights searches (SerpAPI, type: "2") — one per leg, with a 20 s timeout and one retry per leg.
  3. Tags every result with leg_index, leg_from, leg_to, leg_date, and city, keeps the top 5 per leg, and sorts legs into the user's journey order before returning.
  4. Any leg SerpAPI cannot serve (timeout, zero results) is AI-filled with realistic estimates (FlightsAgent._ai_fill_legs, marked source: "estimate"), so no leg ever shows an empty row.

If SerpAPI is unavailable entirely, the AI agent produces all legs from a prompt that lists each leg explicitly and demands leg_index per result; FlightsAgent._group_legs regroups the flat output into ordered legs.

The UI renders one group per leg ("Leg 1 · NYC → Paris · Sep 10") and lets you pick one flight per leg, with a running total for the chosen combination.

docs.title: Every section covers every stop
docs.text:
Specialist prompts carry a mandatory coverage block with per-city quotas so no stop is skipped:

Section Per-city quota Places to See 4–6 (with per-city Serper search context) Walking Tours each city crawled separately, topped up to ≥ min(4, available) Activities ≥ 5 Hotels ≥ 3 What's On (events) 2–4 Getting Around intra-city options per city + inter-city hops (train/bus/flight)

Every result carries a city field, rendered as a 📍 city chip on each card so items are easy to attribute at a glance.

docs.title: Journey order is guaranteed, twice
docs.text:
LLM output order is not trusted:

  • Backend — flight legs are sorted by leg_index; weather days are sorted by (stay order, date).
  • Frontend — orderSectionByCity (frontend/src/utils/orderSectionByCity.js) stable-sorts every city-tagged section list by the index of its city in your entered stop order, the moment results arrive.

The itinerary agent is instructed to visit cities in exactly the order requested — it never reorders your route.

docs.title: Weather per stay
docs.text:
WeatherAgent forecasts each city only for the dates you are actually there:

  • Trips starting within 16 days use the Open-Meteo forecast per stay (free, no key needed).
  • Further-out trips fall back to one LLM climate-estimate call covering all stays. The parser tolerates the model nesting output per city (_flatten_days), assigns each day's city authoritatively from the stay date ranges, dedupes hand-over dates, and sorts by stop order.

The UI groups day cards under a 📍 header per city, in journey order.

docs.title: Visas across countries
docs.text: For multi-country routes the visa agent evaluates entry requirements for every country on the itinerary against your nationality, residence permits, and existing visas — not just the first stop.

docs.title: Notifications API
docs.text:
Frozen with Phase 6 wave 0. Changes: later changes are additive only (new fields, endpoints, categories, kinds or error codes; nothing renamed, removed or re-typed). Every change needs a contract-change note in its PR and an update to this page in the same PR.

Notifications 2.0 adds server-side categories, quiet hours and a daily cap, localized trip-phase pushes (T-30, T-7, T-1 and a morning brief), a shared text catalog for on-device notifications, and APNs for iOS next to FCM for Android. It is additive to /api/notifications*, /api/devices* and /api/alerts/preferences, which keep their request fields, response keys and semantics.

docs.title: API contract
docs.text: All paths are under /api, with JSON in and out. Every route needs Authorization: Bearer <access_token> and acts only on the caller's data. Errors use the Phase 1 envelope {"detail", "error_code"}.

docs.title: Discovery (additive)
docs.text: GET /config gains features.notifications_api: 1 (the routes below exist), features.notifications_v2: bool (NOTIFICATIONS_V2_ENABLED, default on: category checks, trip pushes and platform routing are active) and features.apns: bool (an Apple key is configured). Clients feature-detect notifications_api and hide the settings UI without it.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
GET /notification-settings:

{"categories": {"price_drops": {"enabled": true}, "trip_reminders": {"enabled": true},
                "morning_brief": {"enabled": true}, "weather": {"enabled": true},
                "nearby": {"enabled": true}, "social": {"enabled": true}, "quiz": {"enabled": true}},
 "quiet_hours": {"enabled": true, "start": "22:00", "end": "07:00"},
 "daily_cap": 3, "timezone": "Asia/Kolkata", "quiet_hours_active": true,
 "push": {"fcm": false, "apns": false}, "devices": 2}
  • categories: all default on. nearby is a client-side switch the apps honour for on-device local notifications; the server never sends it. social (idea saved, new follower) and quiz (head-to-head invite, head-to-head result) are sent by the server; quiz kinds are never sent to a user who hides the game. Additive: new notification kinds social_idea_saved, social_new_follower, quiz_h2h_invite, quiz_h2h_result; their text carries no handles or ids. Also additive: social_idea_liked and social_idea_comment (category social; sent to the idea's author, never for one's own action or across a block, at most one of each per idea per UTC day, only for published comments; link /feed) and quiz_daily (category quiz; a once-per-local-day reminder at 12:00-20:00 in the user's timezone, only for users who played in the last 30 days and still have today's daily quiz open; never when the game is hidden or PLAY_ENABLED/GAME_ENABLED are off; link /play). Clients must ignore kinds they do not know. The catalog gains the matching social_idea_liked, social_idea_comment and quiz_daily templates in the 7 languages.
  • quiet_hours is the same value as alert_prefs.quiet_hours (GET/PUT /alerts/preferences): a change through either route shows in both. It is evaluated in the account timezone; timezone is null when unset or invalid, and then quiet hours are not applied and the morning brief is skipped.
  • daily_cap (1 to 10, default 3) counts non-price pushes per user per local day. Price drops are exempt and keep the per-kind caps of /alerts/preferences.
  • push.fcm / push.apns: whether the server can deliver to that platform. devices: the caller's registered device count.

PUT /notification-settings takes any subset of categories.<name>.enabled (bool), quiet_hours (enabled, start, end, as in /alerts/preferences) and daily_cap, and answers with the full object above. timezone, quiet_hours_active, push and devices are read-only and ignored. Failures answer 422 notification_settings_invalid (unknown category or key, wrong type, bad HH:MM, cap outside 1 to 10).

docs.title: Text catalog
docs.text: GET /notifications/catalog?locale=xx answers {"locale": "es", "templates": {"nearby_arrival": "Estás cerca de {place}: {item} está a {minutes} min", ...}}: every template the server sends plus on-device ones, with {name} placeholders. locale is en es de fr hi zh bn; an unknown or missing locale answers en (the response's locale says which). Template keys: trip_t30, trip_t7, trip_t1, trip_morning, nearby_arrival. New keys may appear; apps ignore keys they do not know.

docs.title: Devices (additive)
docs.text: POST /devices accepts platform: "android" | "ios" (an iOS token is the APNs device token as a hex string). Existing android registrations are unchanged.

docs.title: Notification rows and push data (additive)
docs.text: Rows from /notifications and the push data payload gain category and plan_id (null for price drops). New kinds: trip_t30, trip_t7, trip_t1, trip_morning; clients ignore a kind they do not know. link is a web path (/trips/{id}, /trips/{id}/today, /feed, /play/h2h/{match_id}) that apps map to a screen.

docs.title: Delivery rules
docs.text: Category pushes: category enabled? then dedupe (one per user, plan and kind ever; the morning brief per plan and local day) then quiet hours (held until the window ends, dropped if held over 12 h) then the daily cap, then send. The in-app row is always written. Price drops: price_drops enabled, then the Phase 3 rules. Text is rendered in the user's language setting, else the newest device locale, else en. With hide_game no game wording appears. Trip pushes go out inside the local day window only: T-30 and T-7 between 09:00 and 21:00 local (retried on later days of their 25-30 and 5-7 day windows), T-1 only the day before the trip, the morning brief (which also covers the first trip day) between 08:00 and 11:00 local; the T-30 and T-7 text shows the days left. An invalid or missing timezone counts as none (UTC for T-x, no morning brief). While NOTIFICATIONS_V2_ENABLED is off (it is on by default) the behaviour is the Phase 3 behaviour unchanged.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text: The server never receives or stores location, and nothing location-like goes into telemetry. Apps must not send coordinates to any new endpoint; "near you" notifications are built on-device from the catalog and the existing POST /nearby.

docs.title: Telemetry
docs.text: notif_settings_view, notif_category_toggle, notif_quiet_hours_change, notif_cap_change, notif_open: see Telemetry.md.

docs.title: Personalization
docs.text: Three layers tune results to the traveller: saved preferences, per-search settings, and the learned Taste Graph.

docs.title: Preferences
docs.text:
Saved per account (GET/PUT /api/preferences, frontend/src/pages/PreferencesPage.jsx):

  • Travel Budget: Budget, Mid-range or Luxury (pre-fills the Search budget as 1000, 3000 or 8000 USD).
  • Identity: nationality and current residence (used as the default departure city).
  • Documents: residence permits and existing visas.
  • Travel Style: interests, the traveller mix and accessibility needs.

Two-way binding (frontend/src/context/AuthContext.jsx): saved preferences pre-fill the Search form on load, and submitting a search writes its fields back to preferences. The app therefore always remembers the latest defaults. A loaded recent search takes precedence over the pre-fill.

docs.title: Recent searches
docs.text: Every submitted search, from the Search form or from the Results page's search panel, is saved to the account (/api/recent-searches): the newest 8, with identical searches merged (interest order ignored). They appear in a collapsible strip above the Search form; see Trip Planning Features.

docs.title: Per-search settings
docs.text:
These are fields of TravelSearchRequest (backend/app/schemas/request.py) that agents receive in their prompts:

  • Serendipity (serendipity, 0.0–1.0), the Search form's "Discovery style" slider: Famous classics, Balanced mix, Hidden gems. At the hidden-gems end, agents prefer local favourites and mark results hidden_gem: true.
  • Pace (pace: relaxed, balanced or packed) controls how densely the itinerary fills each day. It has no control on the Search form: the "Slow it down" remix sets it to relaxed, and API callers can set it directly.
  • Traveller mix: adults (18–64), seniors (65+), children (5–17), infants (0–4). It shapes fare notes, hotel suitability and activity choices.
  • Accessibility needs: wheelchair, visual, hearing, cognitive. They are passed into every agent prompt.
  • Interests: activities get a model-assigned relevance score (0.0–1.0) and are sorted by it.

docs.title: Taste Graph
docs.text:
The Taste Graph (backend/app/db/taste_db.py) learns a user's style from what they save into plans, with no forms to fill.

  1. Saving a plan (POST/PUT /api/plans) mines its selections for signals (extract_signals): flight style (non-stop or cheapest, per selected leg), hotel tier and type, activity categories and budget band. They are stored in the taste_signals table.
  2. derive_taste_context() condenses the signals into a short sentence, for example "Prefers non-stop flights, mid-range boutique hotels, food and history activities."
  3. On /api/search (with a valid token), /api/chat and their specialist runs, the server sets TravelSearchRequest.taste_context from the user's profile; a value sent by the client is ignored.

Agents use it to rank matching options higher, never to filter options out, so all budget tiers still appear. Because taste_context is part of the search cache key, cached results are per profile and never leak between users.

The Preferences page shows what has been learned (GET /api/taste-profile) and has a Reset button (DELETE /api/taste-profile).

docs.title: Place and Airport Data
docs.text: Travel Planner turns whatever the user types ("Milano", "Portland, ME", "Zermatt") into airport codes for live flight search, and offers an airport-and-place typeahead. Both run against open data committed to the repo and seeded into SQLite. No web call is involved, except for one narrow case described under Bare airport codes.

docs.title: Sources and licences
docs.text:
Source Files used Licence OurAirports airports.csv, regions.csv, countries.csv Public domain GeoNames cities1000.txt, admin1CodesASCII.txt, allCountries.zip CC BY 4.0

Attribution: Contains data from GeoNames (geonames.org), CC BY 4.0. The GeoNames data has been modified (filtered, name-folded, scored and linked to airports; country names, non-town features and districts extracted; a suburb flag derived), and GeoNames does not endorse these changes. Airport data comes from OurAirports. In countries.csv the code and name columns are OurAirports data and the names and qualifier_names columns GeoNames data.

The app footer shows "Place data © GeoNames (CC BY 4.0) · Airport data: OurAirports". backend/app/db/data/README.md holds the full source, licence and derivation notes.

Snapshot date: 2026-10-29 for OurAirports, cities1000 and admin1CodesASCII; 2026-10-30 for allCountries.

docs.title: Committed files
docs.text:
backend/app/db/data/:

File Size Contents airports.csv 347 KB 4,014 airports (4,010 with scheduled service): iata, icao, name, city, country, country_code, region, type_rank, scheduled, lat, lng places.csv.gz 5.6 MB 162,014 GeoNames places with at least 1,000 people (excluding sections of places and historical, abandoned or destroyed places), each linked to up to 3 ranked airports, with folded alternate names for places of 15k or more and a satellite flag (see Suburbs) features.csv.gz 1.7 MB 31,995 notable GeoNames features that are not towns (islands, parks, resorts, regions, mountains, glaciers, caves, lakes, sites…) and famous districts, each with up to 3 airports admin1.csv 121 KB 3,865 first-level divisions (states, provinces, regions) countries.csv 265 KB Every OurAirports country, with 18,071 native and other-language names from GeoNames (and 99 qualifier-only ones) ("Deutschland", "Brasil", "Nippon") hints.json 15 KB Hand-curated, not generated (see below) README.md 10 KB Sources, licences, derivation rules, regeneration, conflict report

The total is about 7 MB (the limit is 9 MB). In addition, backend/app/db/seed_airports.py holds a curated list of 402 airports with served-city overrides, and REPLACED_CODES maps 14 retired codes to their replacements (for example PNH → KTI).

docs.title: hints.json
docs.text:
Curated knowledge the open data lacks:

Key Entries Purpose islands 106 Islands and their airports ("Sicily" and "Sardegna" → CTA, PMO, TPS / CAG, OLB, AHO; "Borneo" → BKI, KCH) destinations 88 Places without a useful airport of their own ("Machu Picchu" → CUZ, "Kyoto" → KIX, ITM; "Zermatt" → ZRH, GVA; "Monte Carlo" → NCE) regions 22 Regions ("Algarve" → FAO; "Lake Garda" → VRN, BGY, VCE) exonyms 80 Other-language or English names mapped to a GeoNames id, or to "ambiguous" ("Cologne" → Köln, "Milano" → Milan; "Odessa" is ambiguous unless qualified) city_aliases 19 Shorthands (SF, LA, KL, HCMC, NOLA…) country_aliases 84 "UK", "England", "Holland", "DPRK", "Eire", and countries' own native names verified against GeoNames, which win over any town of that name ("Deutschland", "Nederland" — not Nederland, Texas —, "España", "Nippon", "Suomi", "Hellas", "Sverige", "Misr", "Maroc"…) qualifier_country_aliases 4 KSA, PRC, ROK, ROC: countries only as a qualifier ("Riyadh, KSA", "Beijing PRC"), because typed alone each is a scheduled airport code (Kosrae, Prescott, Rockhampton, Rochester) saint_exceptions 2 Names that must not get St/Saint variants

docs.title: Regenerating the data
docs.text:
backend/scripts/build_place_data.py is standard-library only and deterministic (sorted rows, gzip mtime 0); it takes about a minute and treats the downloaded sources as untrusted input. Download the OurAirports CSVs and GeoNames cities1000.zip / admin1CodesASCII.txt / allCountries.zip (423 MB, streamed, not unzipped) into a directory of their own, then from the repo root:

python3 -I backend/scripts/build_place_data.py \
    --ourairports /path/to/ourairports-src \
    --geonames-cities /path/to/geonames-src/extracted/cities1000.txt \
    --geonames-admin1 /path/to/geonames-src/admin1CodesASCII.txt \
    --geonames-all /path/to/geonames-src/allCountries.zip \
    --out backend/app/db/data > conflicts.txt

The script writes airports.csv, places.csv.gz, admin1.csv, countries.csv and features.csv.gz, and prints a summary and a conflict report to stdout (not committed). Then run python3 -m pytest tests/test_build_place_data.py from backend/, update the snapshot date in the data README, and commit the five files. The data README holds the derivation rules, including the notability threshold calibration for features. hints.json is edited by hand.

docs.title: Versioned seeding
docs.text:
At startup, seed() in backend/app/db/seed_airports.py loads the files into the airports, places, place_names, features, feature_names and admin1 tables of $DATA_DIR/airports.db. feature_names holds each feature's name, its ASCII spelling and both without a generic part ("Kakadu National Park" → "kakadu", "Mount Everest" → "everest") as tier 0, and its alternate names as tier 1.

  • The data version is the sha256 of a loader tag (place-data-loader:3) plus the bytes of airports.csv, places.csv.gz, admin1.csv and features.csv.gz, truncated to 16 hex characters and stored as meta.place_data_version. An older places table gains its satellite column in place.
  • If the stored version matches, seeding is skipped (about 5 ms).
  • Otherwise one BEGIN IMMEDIATE transaction (waiting up to 30 s for another worker's lock) upserts the airports, sets scheduled = 0 on old rows missing from the dataset, and rebuilds places, place names and divisions with their indexes. On an empty database this takes about 2.5 s and produces about 316,000 place-name rows, 113,000 feature-name rows and a database of about 33 MB.
  • Backups leave these tables and the version out, so a restored database reseeds them.

It can also be run by hand: cd backend && python -m app.db.seed_airports. After seeding, places_db.warm() builds an in-memory airport-name index (about 0.06 s).

docs.title: How a typed place resolves
docs.text: lookup_city_iata(text) (backend/app/db/database.py) returns up to 3 comma-joined scheduled airport codes, best first, or None. The request validator (backend/app/schemas/request.py) uses it to fill origin_iata and destination_iata for flight search, the fare calendar and Compare. When it returns None, flights fall back to AI estimates for that route.

docs.title: The rules, in order
docs.text:
1. An airport code. An upper-case three-letter code is used as typed, after mapping retired codes ("LHR" → LHR, "PNH" → KTI). Lower-case text tries places first and falls back to the code only if it is a scheduled airport ("lhr" → LHR).
  2. A typeahead label such as "LGW — London, United Kingdom" uses its code alone.
  3. A curated hint: an island, destination or region from hints.json, unless a stated country contradicts it.
  4. The curated city list: airports whose served city matches the text (accent-folded, with St/Saint variants and city aliases), restricted by any stated country, ISO code, alias or region code. A city name that is ambiguous or contested gives None.
  5. GeoNames place resolution (resolve_place, backend/app/db/places_db.py):
  6. Candidates are places whose own name matches. Alternate names count only when no place has that own name, or when the own-name places are small (under 20k) and the alternate one is at least 10× bigger and 150k or more.
  7. Exonyms from hints.json map an English name to a specific place, or mark it ambiguous.
  8. A country typed alone gives its top place; a first-level division ("Florida", "Scotland") joins as its top place unless a town of that name is comparably notable. Country names include the native and other-language names in countries.csv ("Deutschland" → BER, "Nippon" → HND); a name that is also the own name of a town of 15k or more stays the town's ("Columbia", South Carolina), unless it is the country's own name, curated as an alias ("Nederland" → AMS, not Nederland, Texas).
  9. Country names that are also a town's own name ("Eretria", "Coria", "Grenade") name the country only as a qualifier; typed alone they stay the town.
  10. Stated qualifiers (country name in any of those forms, ISO code, alias, a qualifier-only alias such as KSA, US/CA/AU/BR/IN region code or a division name) filter the candidates ("Berlin, Deutschland", "Riyadh, KSA"). A qualifier that contradicts every candidate gives None.
  11. An airport whose whole name equals the text can win ("Wagga Wagga" → WGA), but never over a place of 40k or more.
  12. Suburbs yield to towns with their own airport. When the top candidate is a satellite and the best candidate whose first airport is its own scores at least 1/10 of it, the satellites scoring above that town drop out ("Peoria" → PIA, Illinois, not the Phoenix suburb).
  13. A namesake with its own named airport. When the top candidate would win without an airport named for it, and one comparable namesake (score within 5×, at least a third of the people) flies from its own named airport, that namesake leads if the top's nearest airport is over 75 km away ("Tongren" → TEN, Guizhou); otherwise the name is ambiguous ("Salisbury").
  14. The winner must score 3× the next candidate (score = population × notability). A place under 15k wins only alone or through a hint; one under 5k with no airport within 100 km gives None.
  15. Non-town features. When no candidate is a town of 15k or more (and no division or curated city has the name), a notable feature by that name answers with its airports ("Kakadu" → DRW; "Arches" → the national park's CNY, not the French village), unless a town of that name lies within 50 km of it (Paros, Naxos: the island town and its airport). Of several features, the most notable needs 3× the next one's notability; otherwise the answer is None, even when small towns share the name ("Mount Olympus": Cyprus or Greece). Districts answer the same way ("Ealing" → LHR, "Manly" → SYD), except by a contested name that many sections elsewhere share: then the answer is None, never another town ("Centar", "Chinatown", "Downtown"). An alternate-name town of 15k or more with at least twice the best feature's alternate names blocks the feature path and competes ("Vila" → Port Vila's VLI, not an Albanian peak); one known only by its people (not by alternate names) must have 3× the people of every town of that name, alternate names included ("Legazpi" stays the Philippine city).
  16. The place's linked airports are returned. With a curated city in the same country they are appended to the curated codes ("New York" → JFK, LGA, EWR); otherwise foreign airports are dropped unless the place has no domestic one.
  17. Last resort: dataset airports whose display city matches.

Text without a comma is also tried as "City, Qualifier" when the last words name a country or region ("Chicago IL", "Berlin Germany"). Generic affixes are retried too ("Zanzibar Island", "Banff National Park", "Tokyo city").

docs.title: Suburbs (satellite places)
docs.text: A place is a satellite when its first airport is not named for it but for a place scoring at least 10× more within 60 km: Peoria, Arizona flies from Phoenix's PHX, while Peoria, Illinois has PIA. "Named" is core.places.is_named_airport: the airport's display city is the place or its name names the place, never distance alone. A deep suburb (owner ≥ 100× bigger) drops out when a namesake that is an ordinary satellite or flies from its named airport scores more ("Pontevedra" → Spain's SCQ, VGO, not the Buenos Aires suburb). A satellite that would win yields to a namesake with its named airport scoring ≥ 1/10 of it ("Peoria" → PIA); comparable namesakes stay ambiguous ("Redmond", "Darien"). Two comparable suburbs stay ambiguous ("Glendale": California and Arizona → None), and a satellite keeps its lead over a far smaller namesake.

docs.title: Non-town features
docs.text:
features.csv.gz holds 31,995 GeoNames features that are not towns: islands, archipelagos and atolls, peninsulas, parks and reserves, resorts, regions and coasts, mountains, ranges, peaks and volcanoes, valleys, lakes, beaches, ancient and historical sites, ruins and monuments, deserts, gorges and canyons, glaciers, capes, fjords and caves, plus 7,306 famous districts that take their city's airports (Ealing, Manly, Frankston, Shinjuku). Only notable ones are kept: at least 10 GeoNames alternate names (5 for parks, reserves, resorts, glaciers, capes, fjords, caves, islands and deserts; such a weakly notable island or desert is dropped when another GeoNames row has its name), and an airport. Names also match without generic words in several languages ("Isola Stromboli" → "stromboli", "Parque Nacional de Doñana" → "donana", "Killington Peak", "Annapurna I"); after an island, park or peninsula affix only a feature of that kind answers ("San Blas Islands" is not Argentina's San Blas). Their airports are those on the island (for islands), then large and medium airports within 250 km, same country first, by distance with a large airport counted at half its distance (Florida Keys → EYW, then MIA; Lake Tahoe → RNO before Truckee). The data README has the calibration (5 → 83k features and 3.6 MB; 10 → 14k and 0.9 MB; 20 → 1.3k).

Curated hints still come first; features answer names the hints do not cover ("Grand Teton" → JAC, "Crater Lake" → MFR, "Mount Rushmore" → RAP, "Tikal" → FRS, "Haida Gwaii" → YZP). Vast regions give a single point, so their airports can be rough (Sumatra → PKU, Pekanbaru); big islands with several gateways are curated ("Borneo" → BKI, KCH).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Results from the current data:

Input Result Why Milano LIN, MXP, BGY Exonym entry mapping the Italian name to Milan Kyoto KIX, ITM Curated destination hint (Kyoto has no airport) Zermatt ZRH, GVA Curated destination hint (no airport nearby) Portland, ME PWM The state qualifier picks Portland, Maine Portland PDX Portland, Oregon dominates by score Valencia None Valencia, Spain and the larger Valencia, Venezuela: ambiguous Valencia, Spain VLC The country qualifier settles it Monte Carlo NCE Curated destination hint New York JFK, LGA, EWR Curated city plus the place's other airports Chicago IL ORD, MDW, GYY No-comma reading as "Chicago, IL" Paris, Texas DAL, DFW Never CDG Springfield None Many similar-sized namesakes Berlin, Japan None The stated country contradicts the place Deutschland BER GeoNames country name Riyadh KSA RUH No-comma qualifier; KSA alone stays Kosrae's code Peoria PIA Peoria, Arizona is a Phoenix suburb (satellite) Glendale None Two comparable suburbs Kakadu DRW Notable national park, no town of that name Everest KTM, LUA, TPJ Mount Everest (a feature)

docs.title: Bare airport codes
docs.text: The one web path: when a request's origin or destination is a bare 3-letter code that is not in the database or REPLACED_CODES, lookup_iata runs a DuckDuckGo search plus an LLM extraction (agent model, llm.generate_sync) to name the city, and stores the answer (backend/app/db/database.py). Everything else is local.

docs.title: Folding and shared rules
docs.text: app.core.places.fold_place (accent and case folding) is shared by the generator and the runtime, so names match the same way in both. backend/app/core/places.py also loads hints.json and defines OWN_AIRPORT_KM = 25 and NEVER_LINK = {"ECN"} (Ercan is never suggested for a place, only when typed). Region code tables for the US, Canada, Australia, Brazil and India live in backend/app/db/airport_regions.py.

docs.title: Autocomplete
docs.text:
GET /api/airports/search?q=&limit= (search_airports in backend/app/db/database.py; default 10 results, at most 50):

  • Matches airports by code, city, airport name or country, plus the airports of GeoNames places and curated hints whose folded name starts with the query ("kyoto" → ITM, KIX, …; "milan" → MXP, LIN, BGY).
  • From the fourth letter, when no town of 15k or more and no curated hint matches, up to 3 notable features whose name starts with the query add their airports, below every town match ("kakadu" → DRW, MNG).
  • A country's other name or alias suggests the airports of the place the resolver picks for it, and keeps namesakes abroad out ("deutschland" → BER, not Deutschlandsberg's GRZ; "nederland" → AMS, RTM). From five letters, a prefix of one country's other names suggests that gateway first (a GeoNames other-language name yields to a town or district whose own name starts so: "jordaa" → Amsterdam's Jordaan, not Jordan) and still lists the towns ("deuts" → BER, then GRZ). Official names still match the airports' country column ("germany" lists German airports).
  • The suburb rule applies to every matched name: a satellite the resolver sets aside ranks just below its namesake, and stays listed ("peori" → PIA, PHX; "pontevedra" → SCQ, EZE, VGO, AEP).
  • Features also match by alternate and short names ("sifnos" → JTR).
  • When the whole query (four letters or more) resolves by its own name to a town of 15k or more, or to a curated hint, feature or district while no real town's name starts so, lookup_city_iata's answer leads the list ("ealing" → LHR before Ealing, New Zealand's TIU; "peoria" → PIA).
  • Alternate names count for places of 100k or more from the fourth letter ("münch" → München).
  • A place contributes only its own-country airports, and only places scoring at least 1/10 of the best match count.
  • Order: exact code, code prefix, exact name, name prefix, then the rest. Lower-case three-letter text that names a place lists the place first ("hue" → HUI; "HUE" → HUE). Within a class, the more notable place comes first, then curated order, then the bigger airport.
  • "Contains" matches are dropped once there are real matches, and unscheduled airports appear only for their exact code.

Each row has iata_code, name, city, country, country_code.

docs.title: Quality
docs.text:
• Golden set. backend/tests/data/golden_places.csv has 736 cases (443 resolution, 275 data, 18 autocomplete; 578 "first code matches", 98 exact, 50 subset and 10 expected None). tests/test_golden_places_runtime.py runs them all and forbids web calls.
  • Fresh blind probe. On inputs not used during development, about 1.7% resolved to a wrong airport. More inputs now resolve to None by design: when a name is genuinely ambiguous, no answer (and an AI-estimated fare) is better than a confident wrong airport.
  • Country names, suburbs and features (2026-10-30). Measured on the five earlier probe sets (2,484 inputs) and a fresh blind set of 451: on the earlier sets no input gained a wrong airport and one was fixed (Peoria); on the fresh set the 8 wrong answers (7 also on main) were fixed. These figures hold for those sets only.
  • Speed. lookup_city_iata takes about 0.8 ms per call at p50 and under 2.5 ms at p99 (warm), so request handlers call it synchronously.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text: Voyager collects usage data, tied to a random device ID (and to your account when you are signed in), so the project can find bugs and see which features are used. This page lists exactly what is collected, what never is, how long it is kept and how to switch it off. The list below comes from the closed event schema in backend/app/telemetry/registry.py: the server accepts only these events and these properties and silently drops everything else.

docs.title: What is collected
docs.text:
Every batch of events carries a small client block. The telemetry tables store no IP address and no user agent.

The anon_id is a persistent device identifier, so events from one browser can be linked to each other, and to your account when you are signed in. (This is pseudonymous, not anonymous.)

The client block:

Field Meaning anon_id A random UUID generated in your browser, stored on the device. Not derived from you. session_id A random UUID for the current visit. platform web, android or ios. app_version The app build. locale The interface language.

Each event also has a timestamp and, when known, the screen it happened on (a route template such as /chat or /share/:token, never the full URL or the share token). If you are signed in, the server stores your account id with the event; if you are not, it stores none.

docs.title: Events and properties
docs.text:
Property values are short tokens (letters, digits and _ . : / -, no spaces or @), numbers, booleans, or one of a fixed set of choices.

Event Properties app_open, app_background, session_start none screen_view route, referrer_route screen_time route, ms ui_tap tid, route ui_toggle tid, route, on ui_change tid, route ui_submit tid, route search_submit mode (search, chat, compare, link or discover), travelers, nights, multi_city search_first_section ms search_complete ms, sections, errors search_abandon ms, sections section_expand section plan_select section link_out section, domain share target, object alert_event action, kind onboarding_step step, action (view, next, skip or done) theme_change theme (system, light or dark) language_change lang (en, es, de, fr, hi, zh or bn) consent choice (granted or denied) feature_used feature, page perf metric (ttfb, fcp, lcp, inp, cls, long_task or cold_start), value, route error kind (js, promise or api), source, status auth_start method (password, apple, google, facebook or github), mode (signin, signup or link) auth_result method, mode, result (ok, error, cancelled, coming_soon, needs_username or pending), code signup_step step (form, check_email, username or done) email_verify result (ok, expired, invalid, used, resent or email_changed) password_reset step (request or confirm), result (ok, error, expired, invalid or used) account_action action (avatar_upload, avatar_remove, name_change, settings_change, export, delete, link, unlink, signout_all, email_verify_request or change_password) quota_block bucket (search, chat, compare, discover, light_ai or import), reason (daily_quota or unverified) game_award rule, points badge_earned badge level_up level game_view surface (account, nav or celebration) play_quiz_start mode (daily, pack, challenge or h2h), pack play_quiz_answer correct, elapsed_s play_quiz_done mode, correct play_h2h_result winner (you, them or draw) play_board_view scope (global or friends)

tid is the stable identifier of a button or control (for example nav.search), never its visible text.

docs.title: Account data
docs.text:
When you create an account Voyager stores: your username, display name, email address and whether it is verified, a bcrypt hash of your password (never the password), your sign-in method and any linked Google, GitHub, Facebook or Apple identity (provider ID and email, plus an encrypted Apple token that is needed only to revoke access when you delete your account), your settings and onboarding answers, your avatar, active sessions (hashed refresh tokens, device name), and your game progress (XP, badges, streaks). Plans, preferences, recent searches, taste profile, feedback, fare and price watches, notifications and registered devices are stored as before. Verification and reset tokens are stored only as hashes.

  • Avatars are resized to 256 px WebP and kept on the server's disk ($DATA_DIR/avatars). They are not part of the GCS backup, which covers only the database.
  • Retention. An account that never confirms its email is deleted after 7 days. Expired tokens are purged hourly. Refresh tokens expire after 60 days of inactivity and at most 365 days after sign-in.
  • Export. Account → Export my data (GET /api/account/export) downloads everything above as one JSON file.
  • Deletion. Account → Delete account (DELETE /api/account, confirmed with your password, or your username if you have none) removes your account and everything in the export, your avatar file and your telemetry events, and revokes Apple tokens. Backups made before the deletion are not rewritten and age out with the normal backup rotation. The last remaining admin cannot be deleted.
  • Daily AI allowance. To apply the daily limits the server counts, per account and per UTC day, how many AI requests you made in each bucket. No request content is stored.

docs.title: Trips, expenses and journal
docs.text:
If you use trips, the server stores them with your account: trip titles, destinations and dates, your prep checklist ticks, expenses (amount, currency, category, note, day), journal entries and moods, your star ratings and notes for places, which places you visited, the countries (and so continents) of trips you checked in to or completed a recap for, and the offline snapshot of a trip's emergency card, currency, visa and packing facts. All of it is included in Export my data and removed by Delete account.

  • Offline packs are kept in your browser (IndexedDB and the cache of the app's service worker), not sent anywhere. They are cleared when you sign out, and when an administrator switches the offline pack off.
  • No location history. A check-in records a day and the trip's city, never your coordinates. Coordinates stored with a place are the place's, supplied by the app.

docs.title: Price alerts
docs.text: Beyond the watches and notifications above, price alerts 2.0 stores, per account: your alert preferences (weekly digest on or off, weekday, whether the digest also pushes, instant alerts, quiet hours, daily caps, grouping window), a savings ledger (one row per observed price drop on one of your watches: the watch, the prices before and after, the currency and the time; drops between observed prices only, never estimates), a queue of pushes and emails waiting for quiet hours or grouping, a record of which weeks your digest was sent, and a cached price tip per flight watch. The weekly digest is opt-in; it is sent to your account email (if verified and the server has SMTP) and shown in the app, and as a push only if you turn that on. Its email carries a stop link. The savings figure is a tally of "drops caught", not a record of what you booked. All of it is included in Export my data and removed by Delete account. The alert telemetry events (alert_story_view, alert_target_set, alert_advice, alert_drop_seen, alert_quick_watch, alert_suggest, alert_savings_share, alert_prefs_change, alert_digest_open) carry only enums, counts and flags, never an amount, a price, a title or a place. Sharing the "I caught $X" card happens in your browser; the server sees nothing of it.

docs.title: Share links
docs.text: A share link is public: anyone who has the URL can read it, without signing in, until you revoke it. A new link reveals only the trip's title, destination(s), number of days and the items you put in the plan. Exact dates, your departure place and your name are hidden unless you tick them (dates: hidden, month or exact; "show origin"; "show my name"). Link previews and share cards show at most the month and year, even with exact dates. Your email, nationality, visas, residence permits and accessibility needs are never included, and neither is anything from your search besides the whitelisted trip fields. The server stores the link's token, its kind, the plan it points at and your choices; it does not count or record who opens a link. Link previews are made by the chat app or network that fetches the page, which then sees the same public text and image. Search engines are told not to index share pages and cards. Revoking a link makes it stop working within minutes (browsers, proxies and the apps that made a preview may keep a copy for a while). Details: Sharing API.

docs.title: What is never collected
docs.text:
The schema has no field for any of these, and the server drops unknown fields:

  • Free text you type (searches, chat messages, notes, names of places you enter).
  • Precise location.
  • Your email address or name.
  • Other people's content.

docs.title: Server request logs
docs.text: Separately from telemetry, the app's request-log line records only the HTTP method, path, status code, duration and username (or anonymous), with no IP address or user agent; uvicorn's standard access log is not disabled in the app container, and it records the connecting client address.

docs.title: Retention
docs.text: Raw events are kept for 90 days in a separate database file on the server (telemetry.db) and are not backed up. Events already sent stay on the server until that 90-day retention ends, even after you switch collection off; there is no way yet to ask for them to be deleted. Daily aggregate counts (events, users and sessions per day, event and platform) are kept longer in the main database and are backed up with the user tables.

docs.title: Consent and how to switch it off
docs.text:
• If your device time zone is in the EU, EEA, UK or Switzerland, collection is off until you choose. Voyager shows a one-time prompt with Allow and No thanks.
  • Everywhere else collection is on by default and can be switched off at any time.
  • To change your choice, use the Privacy choices link in the footer of any page (including the sign-in page and shared trip pages, so it works without an account), or, when signed in, open Preferences, then Privacy, and use the Help improve Voyager switch.
  • Choosing No thanks (or switching it off) stops collection and clears any events still waiting on your device. The denial itself is stored only on your device; nothing is sent about it.
  • The same switch covers the app's older feature-usage log (POST /api/analytics/events, which records the feature, page and your username in the server log when you are signed in): while collection is off, nothing is sent there either.
  • Telemetry can also be disabled on a self-hosted server with TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false.

docs.title: Setup and Installation
docs.text: How to run Travel Planner on your own machine. There is no hosted instance any more (see Deployment), so this is also how to try the app.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.12 (the Dockerfile and CI use 3.12; pyproject.toml allows 3.11 or later).
  • Node.js 20 (the Dockerfile and CI use 20; vitest 4 needs ^20 || ^22 || >=24 and jsdom 27 needs 20 or later).
  • An LLM.
